implementation_notes: C++11 contextual conversion to bool is the language absorbing the idiom: `explicit operator bool` is considered in `if`, `while`, `!`, `&&`, `||` and ternary conditions, but not for copy-initialization, so `bool n = x;` is an error and the object never promotes to int afterwards - `x + 1`, `x < 42`, `int i = x` and `delete x` do not compile, while `if (x)` and `static_cast<bool>(x)` do. It replaces both the pointer-to-member safe-bool trick and the old `operator void*` used by streams; for generic code, the standard's exposition-only boolean-testable concept (P1964R2) describes the same requirement for values returned by predicates and comparisons, so constraints should demand a boolean-testable result rather than a bare `convertible_to<bool>`.
pitfalls: `explicit operator bool` is not used for implicit conversions in comparison expressions, so the pre-C++11 `if (ptr == 0)` pattern stops compiling (Qt hit this migrating QScopedPointer, QSharedPointer and QWeakPointer) - add explicit `nullptr` comparison overloads before switching.
Do not combine the bool conversion with comparison operators or a second implicit conversion: the overload set grows silently and diagnostics become unreadable; scope comparisons to the type itself.
`operator!` alone is not the pattern: `!x` works but `if (x)` still fails - provide the bool conversion or a named predicate, not just negation.

In generic code a type with explicit `operator bool` may model `convertible_to<bool>` yet fail boolean-testable when viable user-defined `operator&&`/`operator||` are visible; constrain on the semantics you actually need.

variants.name: pointer-to-member safe-bool base (pre-C++11)
variants.implementation_notes: Pre-C++11 realization from Karlsson's article: convert to a pointer to a private member function (`ok_ ? &Testable::this_type_does_not_support_comparisons : 0`). Pointers to members are testable in a condition but are excluded from arithmetic and from implicit conversion to integral types, so `if (x)` works while `x < 42`, `x == other` and `delete x` fail. Free `operator==`/`operator!=` templates that call a non-public member turn accidental cross-type comparisons into compile errors with a readable message; Boost.SmartPtr's operator_bool machinery and Qt's RestrictedBool typedef are library forms of exactly this trick. Use only when the toolchain cannot use C++11.
pitfalls: Convenience hacks leak other conversions: a nested Tester struct or `operator void*` either permits `delete x` or accepts operations the pattern was meant to block; the pointer-to-member type is chosen because it has neither arithmetic nor integral promotion.
The access-control trick is load-bearing: if `this_type_does_not_support_comparisons` becomes reachable, the guard templates compile and accidental comparisons come back.
Member-function-pointer indirection had a measurable cost on some older compilers; the later adjustment was to use a pointer to a member data object instead (Karlsson).
